questions.topic: validity of syllogisms with universal and existential premises
questions.solutionIndependentCheck: An ignorant human exists. Since every human is a thinker, that witness is an ignorant thinker. In (b), a one-person model with a human who is both ignorant and a thinker satisfies both premises, but refutes the conclusion that no human is ignorant.

questions.topic: validity of arguments and the existential nature of a countermodel
questions.solutionIndependentCheck: Statement (a) says the conclusion is always true in a valid argument, without restricting to valuations satisfying the premises. Counterexample: p entails p but p may be false. Statement (b) says every valuation satisfying the premises of an invalid argument makes its conclusion false. Counterexample: p does not entail q; both p=1,q=0 and p=1,q=1 satisfy p, but the conclusion is true in the latter.

questions.topic: restricted quantification and nested implication in a natural-language translation
questions.solution: No unique single-option answer established from the printed question: options 1 and 4 are logically equivalent under the standard parsing.
questions.solutionIndependentCheck: Option 1 is forall x[(S(x) and T(x)) -> forall y(Q(y) -> A(x,y))]. Option 4 is forall x[(S(x) and exists y(Q(y) and not A(x,y))) -> not T(x)]. By De Morgan and contraposition both equal forall x[not S(x) or not T(x) or forall y(Q(y) -> A(x,y))]. The Persian only-if wording also permits a different direction. Official key/author clarification not located.
Not forall x exists y p(x,y) is exists x forall y not p(x,y). A single x has no successful y.
